To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) agricultural extension expenditure is not significantly related to the rate of increase in agricultural output; and (2) the rate of increase of agricultural output is significantly related to the level of agricultural research expenditure.

(1) the average rate of return to research and extension is 30 per cent, (2) the rate of return to extension is 20 per cent, (3) the rate of increase in agricultural output due to research is about 1.5 per cent per annum, and (4) the rate of growth in agricultural production due to extension is about 1 per cent per annum.
(1) the impact of research expenditure on crop productivity is negative, and (2) the impact of extension expenditure on crop productivity in the Punjab is positive.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of research and extension on the productivity of agriculture in Pakistan.
the impact of agricultural extension and research expenditures on crop yields.
the impact of agricultural research and development expenditure in the public sector on agricultural output in Pakistan.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no evidence to suggest that research or extension expenditure has had a positive or negative impact on agricultural output in Pakistan during the period 1965–80.
there is no evidence of a positive impact of research and development expenditures on agricultural productivity in Pakistan.
there has been no impact of research and development expenditure on agriculture in Punjab.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the paper published in this journal by Khan and Akbary is a poor example of research.
agricultural research and extension have had a very positive effect on crop productivity in Punjab, and that the effect of research is greater than that of extension.
the paper by Khan and Akbani suffers from the same kind of methodological problems that were identified in a previous study on the same subject by the same authors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Khan and Akbaris' conclusions should not be accepted as a basis for agricultural policy in Pakistan.
the Khan and Akbaris' results are not robust to alternative specifications and that the impact of agricultural research and development expenditure is not statistically significant in Pakistan.
there is no evidence that research and extension have a positive and significant impact on crop productivity.
